title: The Triple R Process Revised: How New Knowledge Has Changed My Instructional Practice
author: Jeannette Symmonds
summary: Symmonds, a first-grade teacher, describes how her literacy practice changed once she moved from balanced literacy to research-informed phonics instruction. She frames her growth as a triple R cycle of reflection, research and refinement, anchored by a college advisor's question about why 'cat' is spelled with a c rather than a k. She argues that teacher knowledge of how language and reading work is what makes any curriculum succeed, since no program fits every learner. She cites Adams, Beck, Shanahan and Moats to justify explicit, systematic phonics, robust vocabulary teaching, content-rich background knowledge and fluency work. Her daily literacy block is offered as a concrete result. The piece is a personal but substantive case for treating teachers as informed adapters rather than program implementers.
points: Teacher knowledge of language structure, such as the c versus k spelling generalization, underpins every instructional decision and must be continually grown.
Her switch from a balanced literacy program to blending boards and phoneme segmentation produced a noticeable improvement for students who were not thriving.
The triple R cycle (reflect, research, refine) treats classroom practice as a hypothesis-testing process informed by named literacy researchers.
No curriculum is perfect, so teachers' refinements to meet learners' needs, not the program itself, determine outcomes.
Her daily block combines blending routines, drills, explicit new-skill instruction and application time, with vocabulary taught for depth rather than a word-wall mention.
quotes: That moment stayed with me because it revealed how foundational knowledge supports our instructional decisions. These are just some of the events that have helped clarify the importance of teacher knowledge in helping students to become proficient readers. These experiences and leaders have also helped me to understand and expect that the teaching profession is going to require my willingness to continually grow my knowledge.

Teachers are inherently reflective. We are constantly thinking about lessons and data and how to make the best decisions for learners in our classroom. This step, no matter if consciously or subconsciously done, is necessary for systems to grow or for our practice to stay relevant.

When I first taught first grade, we were using a balanced literacy program, but I quickly realized it wasn’t meeting the needs of all my learners. It was like giving everyone the same shoe size and wondering why some kids tripped while others sprinted.

There is no perfect curriculum. What makes the curriculum work is the knowledge that educators bring to the instruction. That is what refinement is. It is the implementation of teacher knowledge which drives instruction.

My literacy block begins with decoding instruction using continuous or successive blending techniques, followed by visual and auditory drills and then rounds out with explicit instruction of new skills, along with time for skill application. This is my daily goal!

Research shows that vocabulary should be actively engaged with, taught explicitly and applied in context. Meanwhile, we are expected to use the word once in a sentence and throw it on the word wall and call it sufficient.
Curriculum writers do not know my students as well as I do. I’m pretty sure none of them have tried to teach a room of a six year olds mid-sugar crash.
